La campana apareció primero como aproxim: The bell appeared first as an approximation to the binomial (De Moivre, 1733) and later in the study of errors in astronomical measurement, at the hands of Gauss and Laplace: hence it is also called the Gaussian. The central limit theorem explains why it comes up so often: when a quantity is the sum of many small independent effects, its distribution tends to be normal, whatever the distribution of each effect. Height depends on many genes and on diet; the error of a measurement, on many tiny imprecisions. That is why the bell is everywhere.
La campana de Gauss aparece en todas par: The Gaussian bell appears everywhere for a deep reason: when many small independent effects are added, the result tends to be normal, whatever the separate causes may say. That is why the heights of a population, the errors of a repeated measurement and the variations of a mass-produced part are all normal. The “68-95-99.7 rule” — the percentage falling within one, two and three deviations — is what makes a quality department talk about “six sigma”.
La campana es simétrica respecto a su ce: The bell is symmetric about its centre, and from that symmetry come two shortcuts that avoid half the lookups in the table. It is worth having them to hand from the start, because they cover exactly the cases the table does not print.

Tipificar $z = \\frac{x-\\mu}{\\sigma}$: Standardising $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ turns any normal into the tabulated $N(0,1)$.
Tipificar es poner en una escala común c: Standardising is putting things measured in different units on a common scale, and that makes it possible to compare the incomparable: if your maths mark is 1.5 deviations above the mean and your language mark 0.8, you have done better in maths even if the language number was higher. The same idea builds the paediatrician's percentile charts and the standardised scores of international tests. And it is the first thing done to data before training any model: [[ia-generalizar|normalising is exactly standardising]], column by column, so that none dominates the rest merely for being measured in larger units. And there is one place where this same formula is used backwards, to manufacture any normal from the standard one: it is the trick that makes it possible to train [[ia-autocodificador|a variational autoencoder]].
Todo lo que sigue son <strong>áreas bajo: Everything that follows is areas under a curve, that is, integrals. The bell is a density function: the probability of landing between two values is the area it encloses between them, and the total area is 1. If that idea is not familiar, the previous topic, [[pe-continuas|Continuous random variables]], builds it up from the histogram. And if you wonder why a table is needed instead of a formula: because this curve has no elementary antiderivative, so there is no way of writing its integral with known functions.
